title: Bash Functions: Args, Exit Codes & Scope
summary: A dense field guide to Bash functions — how arguments arrive, why return codes and stdout are two separate channels, what `local` really scopes, and everything a subshell silently throws away.

chapters.title: What a Bash Function Really Is
points: Definition: a named block of commands stored in shell memory, run in the *current* shell process — not a new process
Two syntaxes: POSIX `name() { ...; }` and Bash keyword `function name { ...; }`; prefer POSIX form for portability
`function name() {...}` is Bash-only mixed form — legal in Bash, breaks in dash/sh
Body must be a compound command; `{ }` needs a space after `{` and a `;` or newline before `}`
`name() ( ... )` with parens makes the body a subshell by definition — every call runs isolated
Functions are looked up BEFORE builtins? No — order is: function, then builtin, then PATH executable. Aliases resolve even earlier, at parse time
Shadowing example: `ls() { command ls --color "$@"; }` — `command` bypasses the function to avoid infinite recursion
`declare -f name` prints the function body; `declare -F` lists names only
`unset -f name` removes a function; plain `unset name` targets the variable namespace first
Functions are NOT exported to child processes by default; `export -f name` puts them in the environment as `BASH_FUNC_name%%`
Definition is a runtime action: a function inside an `if` branch only exists after that branch executes
Functions may be redefined freely — last definition wins, no error, no warning
`type -t name` returns `function`, `builtin`, `alias`, `file`, or `keyword` — the fastest way to see what a word actually is
Comparison row: function = zero fork, same shell state | script = fork + exec, own process, own everything

chapters.title: Arguments: How They Arrive
points: Function args are positional parameters `$1 $2 ...` — they SHADOW the script's own `$1 $2` for the duration of the call
`$0` is the exception: it stays the script/shell name, it is NOT the function name
`FUNCNAME[0]` gives the current function's name; `FUNCNAME` is a whole call-stack array
`$#` = argument count; `$@` and `$*` = all args
`"$@"` expands to separate quoted words; `"$*"` joins into ONE word using first char of `IFS`
Golden rule: always write `"$@"` with quotes — bare `$@` word-splits and glob-expands every arg
`shift` drops `$1` and renumbers; `shift 2` drops two; `shift` past `$#` returns non-zero
Defaults: `local name="${1:-anon}"` uses `anon` when `$1` unset OR empty; `${1-anon}` only when unset
Required-arg guard: `local f="${1:?path required}"` aborts with a message if missing
`${10}` needs braces — `$10` parses as `$1` followed by literal `0`
Passing an array: `f "${arr[@]}"` flattens to N args; there is no true array parameter
Bash 4.3+ nameref: `local -n out=$1` lets the caller pass a variable *name* to be written into
Call syntax has no parentheses and no commas: `greet Bob 42`, never `greet(Bob, 42)`
Args with spaces need quoting at the CALL site too: `f "$file name"` — quoting inside the function cannot recover words already split
`set -- a b c` inside a function rewrites its positional params without touching the caller's

chapters.title: Return Codes: The Status Channel
points: `return N` sets the function's exit status; N is 0–255, truncated modulo 256 (`return 300` yields 44)
Convention: 0 = success, non-zero = failure. Inverted vs. C/Python truthiness — 0 is 'true' in shell
Bare `return` (no argument) returns the status of the LAST command executed in the function
Falling off the end of a function does the same as bare `return` — implicit last-command status
`$?` holds the status of the most recent foreground command; read it IMMEDIATELY, any command overwrites it
`return` vs `exit`: `return` leaves the function; `exit` kills the whole shell/script — a common accidental script-killer
`return` outside a function or sourced file is an error: 'return: can only `return' from a function or sourced script'
Predicate pattern: `is_root() { [[ $EUID -eq 0 ]]; }` — no explicit return needed, the test's status becomes the function's
Direct use in control flow: `if is_root; then ...`, `is_root && setup`, `while has_more; do ...`
Negation: `if ! validate "$f"; then` — `!` inverts the status
`local x=$(cmd)` DESTROYS the exit status — `local` is itself a command and always returns 0. Split it: `local x; x=$(cmd) || return 1`
Standard code meanings: 1 generic error, 2 misuse of builtin, 126 not executable, 127 command not found, 128+N killed by signal N
`return -1` becomes 255 — usable but non-obvious; prefer explicit small codes
Multiple exit codes for meaning: 0 found, 1 not found, 2 bad input — document them in a comment above the function

chapters.title: Output: The Data Channel
points: Functions 'return' data by WRITING to stdout; the caller captures with `result=$(f)` command substitution
Command substitution runs the function in a SUBSHELL — variable changes inside are lost, but stdout comes back
`$(...)` strips ALL trailing newlines from the captured output
Two channels, one call: `out=$(f) ; status=$?` — data on stdout, success on the status code
Send diagnostics to stderr so they don't pollute the captured value: `printf 'warn: %s\n' "$msg" >&2`
`echo` is unreliable for data — mangles leading `-` and interprets backslashes in some shells; use `printf '%s\n' "$x"`
Never mix logging and results on stdout — the classic 'my variable has the log line in it' bug
Multi-value output: print one item per line, caller uses `mapfile -t arr < <(f)` to read into an array
`mapfile < <(f)` (process substitution) keeps the caller's shell as the reader; `f | mapfile` puts mapfile in a subshell and loses the array
Nameref alternative avoids the fork entirely: `f() { local -n r=$1; r=value; }` then `f out; echo "$out"`
Global-variable convention: set `REPLY` (what `read` and `select` use) — no subshell, no fork, but not reentrant
Comparison row: `$(f)` = clean, composable, costs a fork and loses state | nameref/global = fast, stateful, harder to nest
Suppressing output: `f >/dev/null` keeps the return code while discarding data
`f | while read ...` puts the *while* in a subshell in Bash's default config — a top cause of 'my counter is always 0'

chapters.title: Local Variables and Scope
points: Bash has DYNAMIC scope, not lexical: a callee sees the caller's locals, and can modify them
`local x` restricts x to the function and everything it calls, then restores the previous value on return
Without `local`, every assignment is global — silently overwriting a caller's variable of the same name
`local` is only valid inside a function; at top level it errors 'local: can only be used in a function'
Multiple declarations: `local a b c` or `local a=1 b=2` — but each `=` value is a separate word, quote them
`local -r x=5` makes it read-only for the function's lifetime; `local -i n` makes it integer
`local -a arr` / `local -A map` declare local indexed and associative arrays
`declare` inside a function behaves like `local`; at top level it is global — a subtle source of surprise
Loop counters and `i` must be `local` — nested loops in caller and callee otherwise clobber each other
`local` masks exit status (see previous chapter) — the single most reported `local` gotcha
Unset semantics: `unset x` inside a function can unset the caller's variable, exposing the enclosing scope's value
Nameref caveat: `local -n ref=$1` fails if the caller's variable has the same name as `ref` — 'circular name reference'; convention is a `_`-prefixed unlikely name
Discipline rule: declare every variable at the top of the function with `local`, treat globals as read-only unless documented
`set -u` (nounset) turns unset variable reads into hard errors — pairs well with strict `local` use

chapters.title: Subshells: What They Are, What They Lose
points: A subshell is a FORKED copy of the shell process; it inherits state, but nothing it changes flows back
Created by: `( ... )`, `$( ... )` and backticks, every stage of a `|` pipeline, `&` background, process substitution `<( )` / `>( )`
NOT a subshell: `{ ...; }` braces, sourcing with `.`/`source`, plain function calls — these all run in the current shell
Lost on exit: variable assignments, array changes, `cd`, `umask`, `set` options, function definitions, exports
Survives: stdout/stderr (if captured or redirected), the exit status, and side effects outside the process (files, network)
`BASH_SUBSHELL` counts nesting depth — 0 in the parent, 1 inside `( )`. Prints your current depth
`$$` is the PARENT shell's PID even inside a subshell; use `$BASHPID` for the real current PID
Classic loss: `cat f | while read l; do n=$((n+1)); done; echo $n` prints 0 — the while ran in a subshell
Fixes: `while read l; do ...; done < f` (redirect) or `done < <(cmd)` (process substitution) keep the loop in the parent
Bash-only alternative: `shopt -s lastpipe` (needs job control off) runs the LAST pipeline stage in the current shell
Deliberate use: `( cd /tmp && do_work )` — the `cd` cannot escape, no need to `cd -` back
`exit` inside a subshell exits only the subshell, not your script — a silent no-op where you meant to abort
Cost: each subshell is a `fork()`. In a hot loop, thousands of forks dominate runtime — hoist substitutions out of loops
`trap` handlers are reset in a subshell (except ignored signals), so parent EXIT traps do not fire there

chapters.title: Errors, Traps and Strict Mode
points: `set -e` (errexit) is NOT inherited into function bodies in every context — it is suppressed for any command in a condition (`if f`, `f &&`, `! f`)
Consequence: a function called in an `if` runs with errexit effectively off for its whole body, including nested calls
`set -o pipefail` makes a pipeline return the first non-zero status instead of only the last command's
`PIPESTATUS` array holds every stage's status: `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is the first command's
Common strict header: `set -euo pipefail` plus `IFS=$'\n\t'` — understand each flag before adopting it
`set -E` (errtrace) makes `ERR` traps inherit into functions, subshells and command substitutions; without it they do not
`trap 'cleanup' EXIT` fires when the shell exits; `RETURN` trap fires when a function returns (needs `set -T`/functrace)
Cleanup pattern: create a temp dir, `trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT` immediately after, so no path leaks
`die() { printf '%s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }` — the standard fatal-error helper
Error propagation: prefer explicit `cmd || return 1` inside functions over trusting `set -e`
`LINENO` and `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` build useful error messages: `printf 'err %s:%s\n' "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" "$LINENO"`
`caller` builtin prints the call stack frame — `caller 0`, `caller 1` for tracebacks
Subshell interaction: `set -e` inside `$( )` applies to the subshell, and its failure only matters if you check the status
Gotcha: `set -e` does not trigger on a failing command inside `local x=$(fail)` — the `local` swallows it

chapters.title: Recursion, Composition and Call Mechanics
points: Functions may recurse; `FUNCNEST` (default unlimited) caps depth — set `FUNCNEST=100` to catch runaway recursion
Recursion needs `local` on every working variable or each frame corrupts the last (dynamic scope has no per-frame isolation otherwise)
Example: `fact() { local n=$1; ((n<=1)) && { echo 1; return; }; echo $(( n * $(fact $((n-1))) )); }` — note each level forks a subshell
Cost warning: recursion via `$( )` forks once per level; depth 20 = 20 forks. Accumulate into a global/nameref to stay fork-free
`FUNCNAME` array is the live call stack: `FUNCNAME[1]` is the caller's name
`BASH_LINENO` and `BASH_SOURCE` are parallel arrays to `FUNCNAME` — index them together for a traceback
Higher-order dispatch: pass a function name as a string and call it with `"$1" "${@:2}"`
Command-table pattern: `case $cmd in start|stop|status) "cmd_$cmd" "$@" ;; *) usage ;; esac` — validate before calling to avoid arbitrary execution
Never `eval "$user_input"` to dispatch — use a whitelist `case` or an associative array of allowed names
Functions can be defined inside functions; the inner definition becomes GLOBAL once the outer runs, not scoped
Sourcing (`source lib.sh`) loads functions into the current shell — this is how Bash libraries work, no import system
Guard sourced libraries against being executed: `[[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} != "$0" ]] || { echo 'source me'; exit 1; }`
`export -f f` plus `bash -c 'f'` works; `find -exec` needs `bash -c` too since exec'd binaries cannot see functions
Pipelines of functions compose fine: `list_files | filter_big | count` — each stage is a subshell, so none can set a caller variable

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Their Fixes
points: Unquoted `$@`: splits args on whitespace and globs them. Fix: always `"$@"`
`local x=$(cmd)` hiding failure. Fix: `local x; x=$(cmd) || return 1`
Using `exit` where `return` was meant — kills the caller's script. Fix: `return` in library functions, `exit` only in `main`
Missing `local` clobbering a caller's `i`, `f`, `n`, `tmp`. Fix: declare every variable local
Counting inside `cmd | while read`: counter lost to the pipeline subshell. Fix: `while read < <(cmd)`
Reading `$?` too late — an intervening `echo` or `[[ ]]` overwrote it. Fix: capture `local rc=$?` on the very next line
`echo` for data output mangling `-n` and backslashes. Fix: `printf '%s\n'`
Returning a string with `return "$str"` — `return` takes a number only, gives 'numeric argument required'. Fix: print to stdout
Forgetting the space in `{ cmd; }` giving 'syntax error near unexpected token'
Defining a function after its first call site in a straight-line script — 'command not found'. Fix: define at the top, or wrap in `main` called last
Trailing-newline surprise: `$(printf 'a\n\n')` yields just `a`. Fix: append a sentinel char and strip it if newlines matter
Name collision with a builtin or PATH command, causing infinite recursion. Fix: call the real one via `command`/`builtin`
Assuming `set -e` aborts inside a function called under `if` — it does not. Fix: explicit `|| return`
Exporting a function then wondering why a *non-Bash* child cannot see it — `export -f` is Bash-to-Bash only

chapters.title: Design Rules and Cheat Sheet
points: One function, one job; name it `verb_noun` (`fetch_config`, `validate_input`) in lowercase with underscores
Prefix library functions to avoid collisions: `mylib::parse` or `mylib_parse`
Contract per function: document args, stdout meaning, and every exit code in a comment header
Status for success/failure, stdout for data, stderr for humans — never overload one channel
Keep functions under ~50 lines; if it needs a comment to explain a section, that section is another function
Skeleton to memorize: `f() { local a="${1:?}" b="${2:-default}"; ... ; printf '%s\n' "$out"; return 0; }`
Prefer `"$@"` pass-through over rebuilding argument lists by hand
Wrap the script body in `main() { ...; }` and end with `main "$@"` — gives predictable definition order and a clean entry point
Avoid subshells in hot loops; hoist `$( )` out and use namerefs or globals when performance matters
Use `( subshell )` deliberately when you WANT isolation — `cd`, `set` changes, `trap` overrides
Test functions by sourcing the library and calling them directly; keep side effects out of the definition-time path
Run `shellcheck` — it catches unquoted `$@`, `local x=$(...)` status loss, and `while read` subshell bugs mechanically
Portability: `local` is not POSIX (though every real shell has it); `function` keyword, arrays, and `[[ ]]` are Bash-only
Final recap table: function = same shell | `( )`/`$( )`/pipe stage = subshell, state lost | `source` = same shell | script = new process
Reach for a real language when a Bash function needs data structures, floats, or error objects — Bash returns bytes and one small integer, nothing more
